name: Low-glycemic / anti-inflammatory diet

lead: People chasing clearer, less red and less puffy skin adopt a low-glycemic diet: fewer refined sugars and fast carbohydrates, and sometimes less dairy or processed food.

Proponents propose that lower glucose and insulin responses reduce hormone-driven oil production and skin inflammation. Wikipedia's acne article reports that several randomized and non-randomized studies found lower-glycemic-load diets reduced acne severity, while links between dairy and acne are described as weak and observational. The sources reviewed include no dedicated trials of a combined anti-inflammatory diet for appearance.

paras: The glycemic index scores foods from 0 to 100 by how much they raise blood glucose, and people use it to choose slower-digesting carbohydrates such as whole grains and legumes over sugary and refined foods. Some also drop dairy or processed foods. It is a long-term eating pattern, and users generally watch skin over weeks to months.

Dietary change is generally low risk, though individual responses to foods vary. Restrictive eating patterns carry the usual nutritional considerations, and some low-GI foods are not otherwise nutritious.

chain: Lower blood sugar and insulin spikes
angle.text: Users favour low-glycemic foods and cut sugar, sometimes dairy, aiming for clearer skin and less redness or puffiness. Steadier blood sugar and insulin are thought to mean less oil and inflammation in the skin. Trials have linked lower-glycemic-load diets to reduced acne.

lead: A low-glycemic or anti-inflammatory diet is an eating pattern people adopt to get clearer, calmer-looking skin. It generally means choosing low-glycemic-index carbohydrates, cutting back on refined sugars and highly processed foods, and sometimes reducing dairy. The goal in appearance communities is fewer breakouts, less facial redness and a less puffy look.[1]

The glycemic index is a 0 to 100 scale ranking foods by how much they raise blood glucose, introduced in 1981 by David J. Jenkins and colleagues. The skin link people point to is acne: reviews of diet and acne describe studies in which people eating lower-glycemic-load diets had fewer acne lesions than those on high-glycemic-load diets.[2][3] A 12-week randomized trial in 43 young men with acne tested a low-glycemic-load diet against lesion counts.[4]

Dairy and chocolate are also discussed. Reviews describe milk, particularly its whey proteins and insulin-raising effect, as a possible contributor to acne, while Wikipedia's acne article characterizes the dairy evidence as weak and observational.[1][3] Omega-3-rich foods are discussed as having anti-inflammatory effects relevant to acne.[2]

paras: No single standard defines an anti-inflammatory diet. In appearance-focused communities the term usually covers low-GI carbohydrates, limited sugary and processed foods and sometimes less dairy. Research reviews of anti-inflammatory eating describe emphasis on fruit, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, legumes, herbs and plant protein, with limited refined carbohydrates and processed red meat.[5]

The glycemic index measures a food's blood-glucose response, and Wikipedia notes responses vary with ripeness, cooking, processing and what else is eaten. It also notes that some low-GI foods, such as ice cream, are not generally considered nutritious.

Users adopt the pattern mainly for acne and skin redness, and some report that highly processed foods are followed by breakouts. A T Nation poster in a 2009 thread described sensitive skin that broke out after very processed food while trying to build muscle.[6] Others in the same community report no clear link, with one 26-year-old describing clear skin and breakouts under the same dairy and grain intake.[7]
Dermatologists, according to Wikipedia's acne article, often recommend a diet low in simple sugars.[1]
A 2007 randomized controlled trial enrolled 43 male acne patients aged 15 to 25 for 12 weeks with investigator-blinded lesion assessment, testing a low-glycemic-load diet.[4]

A 2022 review summarizes data that a high-glycemic-index diet may trigger acne and that people eating low-glycemic-index diets have fewer lesions, and discusses milk, chocolate, omega-3 fatty acids, hyperinsulinism and IGF-1.[2] A 2021 review likewise reports that people with acne on low-glycemic-load diets had fewer lesions than those on high-glycemic-load diets, that whey proteins may contribute to milk's effect, and that fish and omega-3 intake and probiotics have been examined.[3]

Wikipedia's acne article reports randomized and non-randomized studies finding reduced severity with lower glycemic load, and describes the dairy evidence as weak and observational, with evidence as of 2014 insufficient to recommend milk restriction. It states that evidence does not support a link between chocolate or salt and acne severity.[1]
Studies of anti-inflammatory diets in other conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis and PCOS, have measured pain, disease activity and insulin sensitivity rather than skin appearance.[8][9]

On T Nation, members have compared insulin responses to milk and low-GI foods, with one post stating that milk has a low glycemic index but a high insulin index.[10] A 2020 poster on the forum wrote about a connection between Western diets, glycemic load and hormonal acne.[11]

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, diet is a frequent topic among people trying to clear acne while training, with some tracking breakouts against foods and others reporting no pattern.[6][7][11]
